title: The Ash'ari school
hookLine: paper and ink, and the speech they carry: the Ash'ari middle way

cards: A printed Qur'an, open on a reading stand. Paper from a mill, ink from a factory, glue in the spine. Every bit of it was made, at a certain time, by certain hands.

Someone opens it and recites, and the voice is made too: breath, throat, a person born on a certain day. So here's the question from the trial again, with the book in your hands. Is the Qur'an created?
Ahmad ibn Hanbal said no, and would not say otherwise. The Mu'tazilah said yes. The school that grew from al-Ash'ari drew a line through the middle.

teach.b: The Ash'ari answer goes like this.

teach.h: THE INK AND THE VOICE ARE MADE.
teach.b: Allah's speech is one of His attributes, and like Him it's eternal, not a made thing.

But the copy in your hands, the ink and paper, the sounds in your mouth when you recite, the memory of it in a child's head: all of that is created. So a printed Qur'an is something made that carries something unmade.
The recitation is yours. The speech is His.

teach.h: AGREE WITH EACH SIDE WHERE IT'S RIGHT.
teach.b: That move shows the school's whole style: take a fight with two sides, and find where each side is right. With the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'aris agree that reason matters and that the things of this world are created.
With the people of hadith, they agree that the Qur'an is Allah's speech and not a creature.
So they're called a middle way, between reason running ahead of revelation and a refusal to reason at all. Over the centuries the school drew names that are still taught. Al-Baqillani argued for it.
Al-Juwayni taught it. His student al-Ghazali, whose books are still read, wrote within it. It became tied especially with scholars of the Shafi'i and Maliki schools of law.
Not everyone accepted it. Hanbali scholars, as we'll see in a couple of days, often kept their distance, and Shia theology took its own road.
But the Ash'ari move is the one to keep: the ink is made, and the speech it carries is not.

how: The Ash'ari school is taught in Sunni seminaries as a school of theology, and Ash'aris hold that Allah's speech is eternal while the written copies and recitations of the Qur'an are created.

o: the Mu'tazili view that the Qur'an itself was created by Allah
a middle way: reason serving revelation, and an uncreated speech
a school of law, beside the Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali schools

p: find where each side is right

games.q: someone holds up a printed Qur'an and asks: is this created? what is the Ash'ari answer?
o: yes, all of it, the speech too.
no, not even the ink and paper.
the ink, paper and voice are made; the speech they carry is not.
games.why: the Ash'aris drew the line through the middle: the copy and the recitation are created, and Allah's speech is eternal.

practice: If there's a Qur'an or any well-loved book nearby, rest a hand on it; if not, rest a hand on your chest.
Notice the made things, the paper, the cover, your own breath and voice, and then what they carry: words and meaning that didn't start with the paper.
Say quietly, the recitation is mine, the speech is His, or just hold the thought that made things can carry what isn't made.
